origin.title: From one gift to a global endowment
origin.intro: At the 1917 Rotary convention in Atlanta, Arch C. Klumph — Rotary’s sixth president — proposed that Rotary accept endowments “for the purpose of doing good in the world.” A few months later, the Rotary Club of Kansas City answered — the seed of everything on this page.

timeline.title: The idea
timeline.text: Klumph proposes an endowment at the Atlanta convention; the Rotary Club of Kansas City donates $26.50 — the Foundation’s first gift.

timeline.title: A Foundation is born
timeline.text: The endowment passes $5,000, is renamed The Rotary Foundation, and gains a Board of Trustees — with Klumph as first chair (1928–35).

timeline.title: Paul Harris Fellow
timeline.text: Recognition for $1,000 of cumulative giving is established in Rotary’s founder’s name — today the movement’s most recognized pin.

timeline.title: PolioPlus
timeline.text: Rotary promises to immunize every child on Earth against polio — a public-health commitment without precedent from a volunteer organization.

timeline.title: GPEI founded
timeline.text: Rotary joins WHO, UNICEF and the CDC to launch the Global Polio Eradication Initiative; the Gates Foundation and Gavi later join.

timeline.title: Peace Centers
timeline.text: The Foundation begins training peacebuilders at university centers worldwide.

areasNote.title: Seven Areas of Focus
areasNote.text: Every Foundation grant serves at least one of seven causes: Peacebuilding & Conflict Prevention; Disease Prevention & Treatment; Water, Sanitation & Hygiene; Maternal & Child Health; Basic Education & Literacy; Community Economic Development; and Supporting the Environment (added 2020–21). Explore each in depth on our About page.

mechanism.title: How the money flows
mechanism.intro: The Foundation’s engine is SHARE — the system that turns club giving into local and global grants three years later, with investment earnings covering the overhead.

steps.title: Rotarians give
steps.text: Every Rotarian, Every Year (EREY) is the culture: in 2024–25, 39.9% of all Rotarians contributed — 452,255 people, averaging $241 each.

steps.title: Annual Fund-SHARE
steps.text: Contributions are credited to the donor’s district and invested for three years. Earnings pay the Foundation’s operating costs, so donations aren’t consumed by administration.

steps.title: The 50/50 split
steps.text: After three years, each district’s total splits in half: 50% becomes the World Fund (Trustees’ worldwide priorities) and 50% becomes the District Designated Fund (DDF) — the district’s money to direct.

steps.title: DDF at work
steps.text: Districts may use up to 50% of DDF as District Grants — block grants for quick, club-sized local projects. The rest funds global grants (matched 80% by the World Fund), PolioPlus (matched 50%), Peace Centers, disaster response, or other districts.

steps.title: Money becomes projects
steps.text: In 2024–25 the engine paid $331.6M in program awards and operations — global grants, district grants, disaster response, a Programs of Scale award and Peace Center support (the per-type breakdown is in the achievements list).

funds.name: Annual Fund
funds.note: Invested conservatively (6.9% return in 2024–25); feeds SHARE.

funds.name: Endowment Fund
funds.note: Principal is never spent — only earnings fund programs. 12.7% return in 2024–25.

funds.name: PolioPlus Fund
funds.note: Every dollar is Gates-matched, then flows to the GPEI.

grantTypes.name: District Grant
grantTypes.text: Fast, flexible, local: clubs decide and act within the year — school repairs, tree planting, health camps.

grantTypes.name: Global Grant
grantTypes.match: 80% match on DDF, 50% on cash (max $400K World Fund award)
grantTypes.text: Large international projects with sustainable, measurable outcomes — sponsored by clubs across borders, aligned to an area of focus.

grantTypes.name: Programs of Scale
grantTypes.text: Evidence-based 3–5 year programs ready to scale — the five winners so far are in the achievements list.

grantTypes.name: Disaster Response Grant
grantTypes.text: Money released within days when emergencies strike.

mechanism.shareExample: Worked example: $100 given to Annual Fund-SHARE in 2022–23 becomes $50 of World Fund and $50 of DDF in 2025–26. If the district puts that DDF into a global grant, the World Fund adds its 80% match — the original $100 becomes roughly $190 of project money.

recognition.title: The recognition ladder: PHF to AKS
recognition.intro: The Foundation honors cumulative giving with a ladder every Rotarian knows — starting with the Paul Harris Fellow and crowning at the Arch Klumph Society.

phfRows.recognition: Paul Harris Fellow — certificate and the iconic pin (est. 1957)

recognition.phfNote: Cumulative giving never expires — every dollar moves you up this ladder. Points you earn can also be transferred to honor someone else as a PHF: the full transfer system is the next section.

societies.name: Paul Harris Society
societies.note: The recurring-giving pledge — an official TRF program since 2013–14.

societies.name: Benefactor
societies.note: Outright, or by naming the Endowment Fund in your estate plans.

societies.name: Bequest Society
societies.note: Crystal honors at $10K, $25K (named endowed fund), $50K and $100K; a $250K+ bequest earns posthumous Arch Klumph Society induction.

societies.name: Arch Klumph Society
societies.note: The highest tier — your portrait etched in the AKS Gallery at RI headquarters in Evanston.

societies.name: Legacy Society
societies.note: Formed 2019 for those who promise the Foundation a place in their will.

recognition.aksNote: AKS members who give an additional $250,000+ may designate a Circle of Honor member — passing the flame to a child, parent, sibling, or friend.

points.title: Recognition points: how clubs mint new Paul Harris Fellows
points.intro: Every dollar a Rotarian gives to the Annual Fund, PolioPlus, the Disaster Response Fund or as global grant sponsorship earns one Foundation recognition point. Points are the district’s currency of honor — transferable, strategic, and the engine behind nearly every “new PHF” ceremony you’ve attended.

earning.label: Annual Fund
earning.text: 1 point per $1 — the source behind most members’ points

earning.label: PolioPlus
earning.text: 1 point per $1 you give — the Gates match multiplies the money, not your points

earning.label: Global grant sponsorship
earning.text: 1 point per $1 of the sponsor’s portion

earning.label: Endowment Fund
earning.text: 0 points — Endowment gifts build permanence, not PHF status

points.ownership: Points belong to the original donor until they are used or transferred — and a Major Donor’s surviving spouse may use them. A member’s available points and PHF level are visible to club leaders in the Club Recognition Summary on My Rotary.
transferRules: Transfers move in blocks of at least 100 points at a time, via the signed Recognition and Transfer Request form.
Only the individual donor can transfer points from an individual account.
Only the club president can transfer points from the club’s account.
Only the district governor can transfer points from the district’s account.
Points may not be transferred from a person to a club or district — only to individuals.
Only individuals can become Paul Harris Fellows; businesses and organizations receive a Certificate of Appreciation for $1,000+ gifts or 1,000+ transferred points.

strategy.title: The strategic playbook — points as encouragement
items: Mint a new PHF: the club transfers 1,000 points to a member who has given $500 outright — their combined recognition amount crosses the $1,000 line, and the pin is theirs.
Match a member’s gift: “give $500 and the club matches it with 500 points” — members who might never reach $1,000 alone cross the threshold, and the club climbs toward 100% PHF status.
Honor a champion: name a spouse, community hero or departing president as a PHF by transferring 1,000 points to them — the classic tribute.
Convert pledges in November (TRF month) and at year-end: districts deploy points to turn goodwill into outright gifts before 30 June.
Lift a club’s numbers honestly: points count toward the club’s recognition totals and Annual Fund goal momentum.

points.recognitionAmount: Recognition amount = personal giving + points received from individuals, clubs or districts. It sets a member’s PHF level and their sapphires and rubies — but points given to you never count toward Major Donor recognition, which requires personal outright giving only.

items.name: 100% Paul Harris Fellow Club
items.requirement: every dues-paying member is a PHF

items.name: Every Rotarian, Every Year Club
items.requirement: $100 per-capita to the Annual Fund, each member $25+

items.name: 100% Paul Harris Society Club
items.requirement: every member gives $1,000+ within the year

items.name: Top Three Per Capita
items.requirement: highest Annual Fund per-capita in the district
items.note: clubs giving $50+ per capita are eligible
